This study examines the production of light nuclei in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=3$ GeV, utilizing a novel coalescence model that integrates both quark and hadron degrees of freedom. The model successfully accounts for the observed yields of protons, deuterons, and $^3$He, as well as their mass and rapidity distributions. Additionally, it reproduces the experimental $A/A_{ref}$ ratios, demonstrating that the formation of light nuclei arises from a combination of quark-level and hadron-level coalescence mechanisms. The analysis further indicates that the coalescence of hadrons serves as the primary source for deuterons and $^3$He, while proton generation is predominantly driven by hadron-hadron coalescence.

The study of exoplanets has evolved from merely identifying new worlds to comprehensively analyzing their physical and atmospheric characteristics. This shift has revealed that planets are not isolated entities but are deeply influenced by their surrounding environments. This review examines the current knowledge of planetary environments, emphasizing how these factors affect planetary atmospheres. We explore the origins of these environments, including stellar winds, magnetospheres, radiation, and plasma, along with their interactions with planetary atmospheres. We also address the presence of moons and ring systems within these environments and their specific roles. Finally, the review highlights the critical importance of multi-wavelength observations and modeling in understanding these complex systems, while noting that the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope will significantly advance our knowledge of planetary environments and their impact on exoplanetary atmospheres.

A graph $G$ is defined as $k$-dispersible when its vertex set can be partitioned into $k$ independent sets. In this study, we determine the dispersibility for specific circulant graphs $C(n; \{1, r\})$ and $C(n; \{2, r\})$, where $1 < r < n/2$.

This study introduces an updated approach to the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula, enabling rapid inversion of large matrices through iterative methods. The core innovation involves solving the linear system $(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T)\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by approximating the inverse $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ and subsequently applying it to $\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T)\mathbf{b}$. The primary contribution is the development of a higher-order approximation for $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$ that leverages the matrix's spectral radius. This method is highly efficient for large-scale matrices, as it requires only $O(n^2)$ operations per update compared to the $O(n^3)$ cost of standard inversion. Additionally, the paper proposes a new algorithm for computing these higher-order approximations that is specifically optimized for GPU acceleration.

We examine the power spectrum of primordial fluctuations within the framework of ultra-slow-roll (USR) inflation, incorporating backreaction effects. Our findings indicate that when backreaction is included, the USR phase becomes unstable, and the power spectrum transitions from the characteristic exponential growth associated with the standard USR scenario to an oscillatory pattern. This behavior is a consequence of the continuous reduction in the slow-roll parameter, which causes the system to shift repeatedly between the slow-roll and USR regimes.

This study addresses the enhanced assortment optimization (EAO) problem, which involves selecting a subset of items to maximize total revenue. We model revenue based on a hierarchical category structure, where each category contains multiple items sharing a common base value, augmented by a unique value for specific products. Customers choose items according to a hierarchical Bayesian multinomial logit framework, which incorporates both the category and specific item attributes. We propose a linear programming formulation for this problem and develop a cutting-plane algorithm to solve it. Additionally, we present a heuristic method that generates upper bounds on optimal revenue and lower bounds on the number of required cuts for the exact algorithm. Through computational experiments, we evaluate the performance of both proposed methods.

The case-based approach serves as an alternative to survival analysis, offering a distinct perspective on survival outcomes. This method relies on categorizing subjects into either "cases" (those experiencing the event) or "controls" (those who do not) at specified time points, thereby enabling statistical comparisons of event rates across different groups. This methodology paper introduces the R package "casebase," which facilitates this analysis. We demonstrate the package's utility through examples drawn from the well-known Framingham Heart Study.

We examine a broad class of multi-loop, multi-scale Feynman integrals that are critical for achieving high-precision results in physics. Specifically, we analyze these integrals using the differential equation method, which involves determining the canonical differential equations they satisfy. This section details the associated reduction procedures, including the construction of a basis of master integrals and the determination of rational functions required to express the system in an $\epsilon$-form. We also provide an in-depth analysis of the numerical behavior of the resulting solutions.

This study evaluates the performance of file-based versus object-based data management within high-performance computing (HPC) environments. The research focuses on the Lustre and DAOS filesystems, contrasting their capabilities in storing and serving data objects. The experiments assess various workload types, including random access, sequential access, and copy operations, with specific emphasis on the impact of object size and the number of concurrent processes. The results indicate that DAOS outperforms Lustre in scenarios involving large objects and high process counts, whereas Lustre demonstrates superior performance for smaller objects and lower concurrent process counts.

The surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption has spurred a corresponding demand for EV charging stations. While the expansion of public EV charging infrastructure is essential to support this shift, it introduces significant grid stress due to the high power demands of charging. To mitigate this, it is crucial to manage the charging process effectively, ensuring that infrastructure usage is optimized without overloading the electrical grid. This paper introduces an online access control mechanism designed for public parking structures equipped with EV charging capabilities. The proposed approach employs a dynamic pricing strategy to regulate charging requests, thereby limiting the number of simultaneous charging activities to protect the grid. Additionally, the study examines the theoretical properties of the suggested mechanism and presents simulation results that demonstrate its effectiveness.

This study establishes the existence of self-dual and self-orthogonal linear codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with the property that no codeword has low weight, referred to as LCD codes with no low weight. We demonstrate that any such code can be generated through a process involving a base code and an iterative extension. Furthermore, we prove that both self-dual and self-orthogonal codes exhibiting this no-low-weight characteristic exist for numerous field sizes and code lengths.

We demonstrate that the Mellin-space representation of gravitational scattering amplitudes can be derived from the same building blocks used in modern amplitude theory. This result is achieved by applying a method involving double contraction to the tensor structure of the eikonal form factor, which is then integrated over the momentum transfer.

The United States' western region is a primary focus for renewable energy expansion, yet the environmental impacts of these new facilities remain uncertain. This study examines the trade-offs between land use and decarbonization by evaluating a comprehensive suite of renewable energy technologies across the entire region. We developed a linear optimization model designed to minimize land consumption while meeting a specific decarbonization target. The results indicate that achieving a 50% decarbonization goal by 2050 requires approximately 10 million hectares of new energy infrastructure, a figure that could rise to 15 million hectares under more stringent targets. This demand for land is largely driven by wind and concentrated solar power, which are the most cost-effective options. The study further reveals that concentrating renewable deployment in areas with high land suitability can significantly reduce land requirements by 10% to 25% for various decarbonization scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate that prioritizing specific renewable technologies within high-yield zones can lower land use by an additional 10% to 15%. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of strategic planning to ensure that the transition to a low-carbon grid does not result in excessive land consumption.

Cluster-randomized trials (CRTs) are frequently employed to evaluate vaccine efficacy. In these studies, entire groups or clusters of individuals are randomly assigned to either an intervention or control arm, and data is collected from every participant within each cluster. This approach is often preferred because it can be more cost-effective than individual-level randomization, particularly when the risk of individual-level confounding is high. This paper examines the critical distinction between two prevalent estimands in CRTs: the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect and the modified per-protocol (MPPT) effect. While the ITT-PE reflects the true impact of assigning a cluster to randomization, the MPP-PE specifically measures the impact of administering the vaccine to individuals within a cluster, regardless of whether the entire cluster was randomized. Consequently, the interpretation of the MPP-PE extends beyond direct biological efficacy to include broader public health implications, such as herd immunity. We provide a formal definition of the MPP-PE, outlining its assumptions and limitations, and demonstrate how it can be estimated using a weighted least squares regression model.

The analysis of the spectrum of the normalized Laplacian matrix is crucial for understanding the behavior of the random walk on a graph. This paper examines the spectrum of the normalized Laplacian matrix for fractal Sierksdink's Mobius Octogonal Network, denoted as $SOMON_{n}$. We establish both the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of this network, which leads to the determination of its eigenvalues for the corresponding normalized Lapacian matrix. Furthermore, we derive several important graph invariants, including the algebraic connectivity, the degree of synchronizability, and the synchronization time. We also obtain the precise values for the total and harmonic number of this network.

We examine a distributed online learning scenario involving multiple agents operating within distinct environments, governed by a shared, unknown, and stationary linear model. While every agent encounters noisy observations, they lack direct knowledge of the global model parameters. The objective is to collaboratively estimate the model to minimize cumulative regret. We introduce a novel algorithm that enables agents to learn the global model parameters without exchanging their local observations, data, or model estimates with one another. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the algorithm's regret grows logarithmically with the time horizon, provided the number of agents exceeds the model's dimensionality. Furthermore, we present an efficient method for computing the final action selection that achieves linear time complexity relative to the model's dimension. Empirical simulations confirm the algorithm's effectiveness in distributed linear bandits.

Electronic Health Records (EHR) are indispensable for patient care, yet their scarcity and sensitivity restrict access, thereby limiting the development of advanced tools like machine learning models. To address this, recent efforts have focused on synthetic data generation, which offers a promising solution for creating high-quality training datasets. This study introduces a novel EHR-synthesizing framework that produces realistic data while strictly preserving the statistical properties of the original records. We specifically present a synthetic dataset for cystic fibrosis, a condition affecting approximately 1 in 2,000 newborns in the United States. This dataset comprises 100,000 patient records, each containing up to 100 fields. Our approach utilizes a two-stage process: first, a rule-based system populates the initial patient data, followed by a generative adversarial network (GAN) that refines the records to enhance their realism.

This study examines the $D^0 \to K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pm \pi^\mp$ decay, specifically analyzing the $K^\mp \pi^\pm$ and $K^\mp \pi^\mp$ subsystems. The analysis utilizes a dataset of $1.0 \, \text{fb}^{-1}$ of $D^0$ mesons collected by the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s} = 7 \, \text{TeV}$. The mass spectrum of the $K^\mp \pi^\pm$ subsystem exhibits a clear $K^*(892)^-(\pm)$ resonance, while the $K^\mp \pi^\mp$ subsystem shows a $K^*(1600)^-(\pm)$ resonance. Additionally, a $K^*(800)^-(\pm)$ resonance is identified within the $K^\mp \pi^\mp$ subsystem. Novelpy is a bibliometric and patent analytics package built on Python that quantifies the disruptiveness and novelty of scientific publications and patent documents. The methods employed by Novelpy are grounded in established frameworks for assessing disruptive innovation, specifically the models developed by A. A. Henderson and K. K. Kim.

This study introduces a method for laser intensity modulation that leverages a nonlinear crystal to convert a pump beam's spatial and temporal variations onto a weaker signal beam via cross-phase modulation. The technique is demonstrated by converting the intensity modulation of a low-power beam, which is induced on a high-power beam by a rotating disk, into its own independent modulation pattern. The signal beam's intensity modulation is precisely controlled by adjusting the relative angle between the two beams within the nonlinear medium. The resulting intensity modulation in the signal beam exhibits a time delay relative to the pump beam, governed by the group velocity mismatch between the two lasers inside the crystal. This approach offers a straightforward and flexible means to manipulate the intensity modulation of a laser signal.

This paper details the inaugural effort to automate the Olympic recurve bow, a task that presents distinct challenges compared to other sports due to the necessity of precise accuracy. We outline a complete system designed to facilitate this automation, encompassing a 3D reconstruction module, a deep learning-based recognition component, a prediction algorithm, and an actuation system. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset featuring 1,000 annotated images of the recurve arrow, and we evaluate our approach using a simulation-based study.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) offers a promising solution to the challenge of data sparsity in recommender systems. However, existing CDR methods often fail to adequately leverage the complementary information found in both source and target domains, leading to suboptimal performance. To address this, we introduce Dual Metric Training (DMT), a straightforward yet powerful framework designed to maximize mutual domain information. DMT operates through two complementary objectives: a standard metric that enforces domain-specific feature separation, and a complementary dual metric that aligns cross-domain representations. By training the model with both metrics simultaneously, DMT effectively captures domain-unique and shared information. Additionally, DMT incorporates a gating mechanism to dynamically select domain-specific data for source domains and target-specific data for target domains, ensuring efficient utilization of available information. Extensive experiments across three datasets demonstrate that DMT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, delivering up to 4.2% and 10.5% improvements in Hit Rate (Hit@100) and Recall@100, respectively.

We demonstrate that the modal mu fragment of distributed mu-calculus can be characterized using a novel class of state machines we call asynchronous distributed machines. These machines are defined as standard finite state machines with input/output capabilities, where communication occurs via a shared memory buffer. This model is asynchronous, meaning the buffer is not cleared after every read or write operation. We further show that the weakest preconditions of these machines can be computed using a specific modal mu fragment of the distributed mu-calculus, a fragment that is significantly smaller than the modal mu fragment.

This study examines the thermal transfer within a two-dimensional complex plasma layer, specifically a system of interacting charged particles in thermal equilibrium. The analysis covers a broad spectrum of temperature and density regimes, with particular attention to the kinetic effects of the Kac model. The heat flux is derived using the Chapman-Enskog method, and the resulting transport coefficients are evaluated through numerical computation.

This study introduces a novel method for aggregating data within unordered vectors, termed the linear composition, which serves as a commutative and associative operation. By utilizing linear compositions, we establish a new framework for calculating the sum of data vectors, diverging from the traditional approach that relies on a specific ordering. This composition is defined through the sum of all possible vector products, weighted by specific coefficients. Furthermore, we demonstrate that linear compositions can be expressed as the sum of specific vector subsets, leading to the development of an efficient algorithm for calculating these compositions. Additionally, the paper explores the relationship between linear compositions and the concept of shuffles, alongside an analysis of their algebraic characteristics.

Fluoroscopic cardiac angiography is a critical procedure for diagnosing and treating coronary artery disease, yet it exposes patients to significant ionizing radiation risks. This study introduces a deep learning-based video interpolation method designed to mitigate patient exposure by reducing the imaging frame rate. The approach utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to synthesize intermediate frames from adjacent images, thereby creating smoother video sequences. We evaluated this method using both a clinical dataset and a synthetic one, comparing it against standard imaging protocols. Results indicate that our approach lowers radiation dose by 50% while maintaining diagnostic image quality. Furthermore, the interpolated videos are suitable for downstream computer vision applications, such as optical flow estimation and cardiac motion segmentation.

The Future Circular Collider (FCC) is a proposed facility designed to operate as a $e^+e^-$ collider with a 120 GeV center-of-mass energy, serving as a Higgs boson factory. It will also function as a proton collider with a 100 TeV center-of-mass energy. This facility is expected to deliver an integrated luminosity of 56 ab$^{-1}$ at the $Z$-pole, 2.5 ab$^{-1}$ at the $\tau$-pole, and 1.5 ab$^{-1}$ at the $t\bar{t}$ threshold. The exceptional precision of the FCC-$ee$ enables the high-precision study of heavy-flavor hadrons, offering significant potential for advancing our understanding of the Standard Model. This paper outlines the opportunities and challenges associated with heavy-flavor physics at the FCC-$ee$.

This study examines the impact of sterile neutrinos on the cosmological relic density of dark matter within leptophilic $U(1)$ gauge models. We demonstrate that the presence of a sterile neutrino can resolve the issue of excessive relic density, thereby establishing a robust upper limit on the gauge coupling. This limit proves to be significantly more stringent than the one derived from the CMB. We further analyze the specific case of the $U(1)_{L_{\mu}-L_{\tau}}$ symmetry, showing that its corresponding gauge coupling is constrained by several orders of magnitude compared to previous findings.

The gravitational influence of a massive central black hole on planetary systems is a significant factor in the formation of exoplanets. This study investigates how secular perturbations from an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) at the Galactic Center (GC) can eject hypervelocity stars (HVSs) from the GC. We model the IMBH as a 10,000 solar mass object orbiting the GC black hole with a 100,000-year period and eccentricity of 0.95. Our simulations reveal that stars within a 1000 AU radius of the IMBH are ejected at a rate of 1000 per year, with a mean ejection speed of 1000 km/s. These ejected stars possess a mean mass of 1000 solar masses and a mean age of 1000 years. The orbital eccentricity of the IMBH significantly affects the ejection rate, with a 1000% increase observed when eccentricity increases from 0.5 to 0.95. Additionally, the ejection rate is highly sensitive to the IMBH's mass, increasing by a factor of 1000 when the IMBH mass increases from 1000 to 10000 solar masses. Our results suggest that the IMBH at the GC is a viable source of HVSs, with the ejection rate increasing by a factor

We examine weak solutions to multivariate stochastic differential equations (SDEs) that are driven by additive Brownian motions and subject to singular drift conditions. The drift is modeled as the sum of a singular term, $b$ (which may be a distribution), and a regularizing term, $\varepsilon$ (which is a smooth function). By demonstrating that the resulting SDEs are smooth for any $\varepsilon > 0$, we establish the existence of a weak solution for the original singular SDE as $\varepsilon$ approaches zero. This approach is demonstrated to be effective for the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in three spatial dimensions.

We demonstrate that the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ is $\omega_2$-tall within any model containing an $\omega_2$-generic filter for the poset $\mathbb{P}(\omega_1)^{\text{NS}}$. This result extends to the poset $\text{Add}(\omega,\omega_2)$, thereby establishing the $\omega_2$-tallness of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ in the generic extension. Furthermore, we establish that the $\omega_2$-tallness of the nonstationary ideal on $\omega_1$ holds in the generic extension generated by $\text{Add}(\omega_1,\omega_1)$.

Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in numerous tasks, they often struggle with the high costs of training and inference, as well as the need for extensive data. To address these challenges, we introduce "Adaptor," a framework designed to adapt LLMs toward specific objectives. Adaptor enhances model performance by leveraging external knowledge, such as retrieved documents or code snippets, and employs a goal-centric strategy that dynamically selects relevant tasks from pre-training data based on user input. We evaluate Adaptor across various benchmarks, including math reasoning, code generation, and question answering, demonstrating that it achieves comparable results to models trained from scratch while using only a fraction of the computational resources.

We introduce the Mapillary Traffic Signal Dataset, a global collection comprising 10,000 images from 100 cities across six continents. This resource supports research on traffic signal detection and classification, addressing a critical gap in existing literature where prior studies relied on limited datasets from single cities or specific geographic regions. Such limitations often result in poor generalization for global applications. To mitigate this, our dataset aggregates imagery from diverse locations to facilitate robust, worldwide traffic signal recognition.

Collaborative filtering (CF) has become a cornerstone of recommender systems, yet existing methods often rely heavily on user-item interactions, which are frequently sparse. To address this, we introduce SelfCF, a new self-supervised CF framework that learns representations for both users and items without requiring explicit interactions. By utilizing a self-distillation technique, SelfCF generates pseudo-interactions to create positive pairs for contrastive learning, thereby enhancing the alignment between user and item representations. Additionally, SelfCF employs a self-regulation mechanism to dynamically adjust the temperature parameter within the contrastive loss, ensuring greater training stability. Comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that SelfCF surpasses state-of-the-art models in both recommendation accuracy and robustness to sparsity.

Tevelev degrees are defined as the count of marked $\mathbb{P}^1$s within a specific divisor class inside the moduli space of $n$-marked $\mathbb{P}^1$s with $0$-torsion, where the level corresponds to the degree. In this work, we extend this definition to include generalized levels for any specified divisor class. We establish that for any class in the moduli space, there exists a generalized Tevelev level that is achieved by a sufficiently large number of marked points. Furthermore, we demonstrate that generalized Tevelev degrees vanish if and only if the underlying divisor class is trivial.

This study examines a gapped Dirac semimetal featuring both linear and quadratic dispersion relations. We establish that the gapless nodes are confined to one-dimensional lines, with the number of these nodes being quantized.

This study demonstrates that for a slow curve in a semi-stable vector field, the entrance-exit map along the curve's slow normal section is essentially a monomial. These fields are characterized by having a specific arrangement of singularities, where the Jacobian determinant vanishes to a high order along a specific curve.

This study examines the detectability of gravitational wave signals arising from binary black hole mergers involving elevated gravitational order modes ($\ell > 2$), which are predicted by scalar-tensor theories. These signals are characterized by a distinct frequency evolution and a specific polarization pattern. We demonstrate that these unique frequency and polarization traits can be identified by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA network during the third-generation era, specifically by the Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope. We further quantify the detectability of these higher-order modes using the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the Bayesian information metric. Our findings indicate that both detectors can identify these signals with a 95% confidence level, provided the primary black hole mass exceeds $100\,M_\odot$. Additionally, we show that the Einstein Telescope offers superior sensitivity to these modes compared to the Cosmic Explorer.

This study examines the astrometric capabilities of the Gaia mission in detecting and measuring the orbits of the Sun's stellar companions. We model Gaia's observational data for a system comprising the Sun and a single companion, accounting for the Sun's orbital motion around the Galactic center, the companion's partial orbit, and measurement errors. We derive the companion's orbital parameters and associated uncertainties using a Bayesian approach. We find that the companion's mass can be determined with high precision, provided the orbit is sufficiently large and the partial orbital arc is sufficiently long. We also demonstrate that the companion's distance from the Sun can be estimated with good accuracy, even when the orbit is highly inclined relative to the line of sight. We also explore the impact of the companion's orbital motion on the Sun's apparent proper motion and its effect on the measurement of the Sun's orbital motion around the Galactic center. The 0/1 Knapsack problem, a classic combinatorial optimization challenge, has been extensively addressed using Genetic Algorithms (GA). This study evaluates the impact of various crossover and selection techniques on the convergence of such 0/0 solutions. We developed a novel approach that integrates multiple crossover and selection strategies, utilizing a specific probability of application for each method during the evolutionary process. Results indicate that this hybridization approach outperforms traditional methods that rely on a single strategy.

This study examines bilinear oscillatory integral operators on the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ that feature a trilinear phase function. We demonstrate that if the phase function possesses nonvanishing linearly independent gradients, then the operator maps $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ into itself boundedly. Furthermore, we provide specific examples of phase functions where the gradients exhibit linear dependence, showing that in these cases, the operator is not boundedly from $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$ to $L^2(\mathbb{R}^2)$.

This study introduces a hate speech detection system utilizing T5, an encoder-decoder Transformer architecture, enhanced with additional data and evaluated through an ensemble approach. The T5 framework was trained on the HateXplain dataset, augmented with synthetic data generated via GPT-3, and subsequently tested on four distinct datasets: HATEXPLAN, HATExPLAN, HATExPLAN, and HATExPLAN. The outcomes demonstrate that the ensemble model outperforms the standalone T5 architecture.

This study examines the scaling characteristics of the density matrix expansion (DME) quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) force for heavy-ion collisions, specifically focusing on the $^{12}$C+$^{12}$C system. We analyze the DME-QMCI's scaling behavior with respect to the number of basis states, the spatial cutoff radius, and the magnitude of the DME interaction cutoff radius. Our findings indicate that the method scales efficiently, with computational costs and force accuracy rising approximately linearly as the basis size and cutoff radii increase. Furthermore, the method demonstrates robustness regarding the chosen cutoff radius for the DME interaction, maintaining acceptable accuracy even at shorter distances.

Social media platforms have become a primary source for identifying misinformation and deceptive narratives, particularly during elections. To address this, researchers have developed various methods for detecting election-related fraud claims, yet most existing approaches rely on limited datasets that fail to account for the diverse ways such claims are expressed. This paper introduces VoterFraud200, a comprehensive multi-modal dataset comprising 11,000 tweets annotated with claims regarding specific election fraud instances. We present a detailed analysis of the data and introduce a novel deep learning framework designed to detect these claims by leveraging both visual and textual information. Our model utilizes a multi-modal fusion strategy that combines features from both images and text to enhance claim identification. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing models relying solely on textual data.

This work investigates the emergence of diffeomorphisms within a random environment, where the associated random compositions are assumed to be $C^2$ and possess positive or non-zero components in their Lyapunov vectors. It is demonstrated that the resulting composition is a $C^1$-diffeomorphism almost surely, and the behavior of its $C^1$-regularity is analyzed.

Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) are increasingly utilized to address complex challenges in machine learning, particularly those involving uncertainty. However, the intricate nature of BNNs often renders their full posterior distributions intractable, necessitating the use of variational inference (VI) to approximate them. This study introduces a novel BNN architecture that encodes the latent posterior distribution using a single neural network, thereby enabling the application of established VI techniques. The approach is validated on a diverse set of tasks, including regression, classification, and generative modeling. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves uncertainty quantification performance comparable to state-of-the-art BNNs, while offering a significant reduction in computational cost.

This work examines the semiclassical instanton framework for Marcus-Levich-Jortner (MLJ) theory, which models electron transfer in polar solvents by incorporating quantized vibrational modes. We derive a semiclassical instanton action for MLJ theory, demonstrating that it yields an electron transfer rate identical to the quantum formulation when the classical harmonic oscillator frequencies approach the quantum regime. Furthermore, we establish that both semiclassical instanton actions converge to a unified quantum instanton action in the limit of high quantum number vibrational excitations.

This paper presents a trajectory control design strategy that integrates the strengths of both optimal and control-theoretic methods. While optimal control offers superior theoretical performance, it often proves impractical for real-world scenarios due to its complexity and the need for precise system models. Conversely, control-theoretic techniques are straightforward to implement but may fall short of the theoretical performance ceiling. To address this, we propose a hybrid approach that leverages the benefits of both frameworks. Our method involves generating trajectories via optimal control and implementing them using control-theoretic tools. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this combined strategy through a simulation of a quadrotor navigating a dynamic environment.

We introduce a theory describing the vast thermoelectric effect in magnetic systems, which operates on a magnon-drag mechanism. This mechanism arises from the transfer of energy between phonons and magnons. The resulting magnon thermal conductivity is calculated using Boltzmann transport theory, incorporating a phenomenological magnon lifetime. The theoretical framework is applied to thin-film Heusler alloys, which exhibit a magnetic transition at 100 K. Our calculations indicate that the effect peaks near this transition temperature, aligning well with experimental data.

This paper presents a probabilistic approach to determining the maximum possible sum from a collection of integers, where each value has a specific probability of being selected. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated through a numerical example, and its computational efficiency is evaluated against a brute-force method using empirical runtime analysis.

This study examines the presence of high-degree elements within finite fields by analyzing binary trinomials over $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$. Specifically, it demonstrates that for fields where $q$ is a prime power and $n$ is a multiple of $q-1$, the equation $x^{q^n-1}-a(x^q-x+1)=0$ admits a solution with degree at least $qn/((q+1)2^q+2)$, where $a \in \mathbb{F}_q^*$. Additionally, it is established that $x^{q^n}-ab(x^q-x+1)=0$ yields an element of degree $qn-2n+1$, where $a,b \in \mathbb{F}_{q^n}$, and the polynomial $x^{q^n}-ax^{q}+b$ possesses a solution of degree $qn-2n+1$.

This paper presents a novel methodology for examining the source code of programs written in C, C++, or Java, which leverage timed automata. Timed automata constitute a subset within the broader field of formal methods, a domain dedicated to verifying software correctness. Our approach offers a fresh perspective on validating source code, a critical step in the overall software development lifecycle.

This approach integrates compressed sensing (CS) with deep learning (DL) to overcome the inherent trade-off between sampling efficiency and image quality. Our system utilizes a DL-based CS algorithm to recover high-resolution images from undersampled measurements, effectively addressing the challenge of limited sampling efficiency. This study investigates the optical Stark effect induced by two-color, circularly polarized laser fields with a frequency offset, focusing on the resulting shifts in atomic energy levels. We demonstrate that this offset generates an AC-Stark shift that varies linearly with frequency deviation, a phenomenon we term a "tilted AC-Stark effect." This phenomenon is particularly significant in high-intensity regimes, where it can substantially alter atomic energy spectra. We further illustrate that such spectral distortions can be detected through the analysis of electron angular distributions generated in strong-field ionization.

This study introduces a new technique for image mixing that combines the semantic content of a target image with the style of a source image. Unlike existing methods that focus on blending pixel-level data, our approach operates at the level of semantic structures. We first extract the semantic content from both the source and target images, then blend these extracted meanings together. The final output is generated by rendering the mixed semantics using the original style image's textures. The result is a seamless synthesis where high-level semantic structures from the source are effectively integrated with stylistic elements from the target.

Stochastic gene expression is a fundamental aspect of cellular function, where the inherent randomness of biochemical reactions influences the behavior of individual cells. Consequently, accurately modeling this process is essential for understanding how single cells operate. This work introduces a computational framework designed to extract key parameters from stochastic gene expression trajectories. The approach employs a two-step methodology: first, it utilizes a variational autoencoder to learn latent representations of gene expression data, and second, it maps these latent variables to the parameters of a chemical master equation (CME) model. We demonstrate that this framework can effectively recover CME parameters from simulated stochastic gene trajectories. Furthermore, we illustrate its utility in analyzing real-world data from a synthetic mammalian gene system, where it successfully inferred parameters for a CME model that closely aligns with the observed dynamics.

This paper introduces a new semi-supervised learning framework that leverages the statistical properties of data. The proposed method utilizes a data-driven, unsupervised approach to construct a manifold, which subsequently guides the learning process by incorporating manifold information into the loss function of a supervised neural network. This integration enables the model to adaptively assign varying degrees of confidence to unlabeled samples based on the learned geometry. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data.

Quantum computers are expected to deliver significant speedups for specific tasks, such as solving linear systems, but their current limitations restrict the size of problems that can be addressed. Consequently, the primary objective is to decompose larger problems into smaller, tractable sub-problems. This paper introduces Layerwise Quantum Substitution Optimisation (LQSO), a technique that segments a linear system into layers, where each sub-layer is solved on a quantum device and the resulting output serves as input for the subsequent layer. We demonstrate that the LQSO method achieves accuracy comparable to the quantum least squares method (QLSM) and the quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). Furthermore, we show that the method can be optimized to reduce the number of quantum queries. Finally, we investigate accuracy degradation caused by the saturation of controlled rotation gates in the LQSO framework.

Re-identification (ReID) is a well-established task in computer vision that involves locating images of a specific individual across multiple camera views. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel challenge termed "individual re-identification" (IRID), which focuses on tracking a single person throughout an entire video sequence. This task is significantly more difficult than multi-camera ReID because it requires matching that individual against every frame in the sequence. To address this, we present a novel framework that integrates a temporal-aware feature extractor with a temporal-aware metric learning module. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the two standard IRID benchmarks, the DukeMTMC-3D and the PRID-2014.

Accurate and precise simulation models are fundamental to conducting cutting-edge research in power systems. This paper introduces a data-driven approach to time series reconstruction, designed to enhance the accuracy of simulations by generating synthetic data that aligns with the statistical properties of actual measurements. By utilizing a generative model, we synthesize time series that replicate key characteristics of real-world data, thereby enabling researchers to conduct rigorous, data-faithful simulations. The proposed framework is validated using a high-voltage transmission network, demonstrating its effectiveness.

This paper examines the behavior of a fixed-point iteration algorithm applied to the variational inequality problem (VIP) involving a monotone operator and a closed, convex set. The operator is subject to a bounded perturbation, and the set represents a closed ball with a perturbed center. We establish the existence of fixed points and demonstrate that every sequence generated by the algorithm converges to the unique solution of the VIP, provided the perturbation magnitude is sufficiently small.

This paper demonstrates that a Fuchsian group is isoxial precisely when the intersections of its geodesics follow a specific pattern. We also provide an explicit geometric method for constructing a hyperbolic surface with cross-ratios equal to one for any points located at the endpoints of these geodesics. Additionally, we present findings regarding the density of such groups within the space of all Fuchsian groups.

This study investigates potential lepton flavor violation in the radiative decay $\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow e^{\pm}\mu^{\mp}\gamma$ using a dataset of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ of $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions collected by the BESIII detector at the BEPCII storage ring. The analysis establishes an upper limit on the branching fraction of $\mathcal{B}(\Upsilon (3S)\rightarrow e^{+}\mu^{-}\gamma) < 1.1 \times 10^{-5}$ at a 90\% confidence level, with no significant evidence of lepton flavor transgression observed.

Theoretical investigations into flat-band systems suggest that superconductivity can emerge in the absence of phonons, driven by the intense electron correlations inherent in these materials. This study examines the pressure-dependent superconducting properties of Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ flat-band compounds, where the Se concentration ($x$) varies between 0.0 and 0.05. Our findings reveal that superconductivity is activated under high pressure, with the critical temperature ($T_c$) peaking at 10.5 K for the $x$ = 0.0 composition at 10 GPa. Notably, the $T_c$ maximum occurs at a composition of $x$ = 0.0, whereas compositions with $x$ = 0.01 and 0.05 exhibit $T_c$ maxima at 8.5 K and 6.5 K, respectively. Furthermore, the $T_c$ maximum is observed at a pressure of 10 GPa for the $x$ = 0.0 sample, whereas it shifts to 6.5 GPa for the $x$ = 0.01 and 0.01 compositions. We examine the path integral formulation of two-dimensional gravity, specifically focusing on the reconstruction of black hole data from observables. Our analysis reveals that the saddle point in the path integral is determined by the black hole's horizon area, which is not fixed by boundary conditions but emerges as a dynamical variable. We demonstrate that the black hole's entropy arises from the logarithmic correction to this saddle point action. Furthermore, we show that integrating over the horizon area yields the microcanonical partition function, while fixing the horizon area recovers canonical correlation functions.

Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (NeuralODEs) have proven highly effective for modeling time-series data. However, real-world scenarios often involve data that is either erratic or contaminated by noise, presenting a significant challenge for these models. This study addresses the difficulty of learning from time-series that are both noisy and irregular. We introduce a new framework that integrates continuous latent representations with discrete observations. This approach enables the modeling of underlying system dynamics while simultaneously handling noisy signals and varying time intervals. We also present a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the proposed method achieves consistent convergence for recovering latent trajectories, provided the true dynamics are representable by a NeuralODE. Furthermore, our experiments on real-world datasets highlight the advantages of this framework over existing alternatives.

Object goal navigation has gained significant attention within the robotics community due to its practical applications. While prior research has primarily focused on learning to navigate toward specific object locations, this study introduces a new approach for navigating based on specific object goals. This method employs a transformer-based architecture to facilitate the long-range modeling of relationships between the environment and the target object. We propose a new architecture called the Object Recall Transformer (OReT), which integrates object-centric and scene-centric representations to enhance navigation toward novel objects. OReT utilizes a dedicated object recall module that enables the encoder to capture and retain critical visual details of the target object. Experimental results demonstrate that OReT surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both performance and robustness.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized for instruction tuning, where they generate outputs based on user directives. However, the computational costs associated with this approach are substantial, necessitating vast amounts of labeled data and repeated model training. To address this, we introduce OPT-IML, a new framework that leverages instruction meta-learning to enhance model performance on unseen instructions. OPT-IML operates by training an LLM to rapidly adapt to new instructions using only a few examples, thereby eliminating the need for extensive retraining. Our method employs a two-stage process: first, a meta-training phase where an LLM learns across a diverse set of instructions to acquire the ability to generalize; second, a phase involving few-shot prompting to apply the adapted model to novel tasks. We evaluated OPT-IML against standard instruction tuning baselines using OPT-125m and OPT-2.5 models, focusing on the task of generating math word problems. Our results demonstrate that OPT-IML achieves superior performance with significantly reduced computational costs. Specifically, OPT-IML outperforms standard instruction tuning by 10.5% in accuracy while requiring 100 times less training compute.

Legitimate Peripheral Participation (LPP) is a concept describing how newcomers join communities of practice by engaging in activities at the periphery of the group, gradually moving toward full involvement. This study examines a large-scale dataset from the Scratch platform, which enables users to create, share, and learn coding through a social, game-based approach. By analyzing over 1.2 million submissions from more than 1.5 million users, we investigate the trajectory from initial entry to full participation. Our findings reveal that the path to integration is not linear; rather, users frequently oscillate between different levels of participation, with repeated cycles common in achieving full engagement. Furthermore, we identify that certain users bypass these peripheries entirely, jumping straight to a central role without gradual integration. These results offer a detailed, data-driven understanding of how LPP operates within a massive online learning environment.

This study introduces a novel approach to calculating the uniform electron gas's correlation energy using perturbation theory. The method employs a unitarily transformed Hamiltonian, where electron pairs are separated by a correlation factor designed to mitigate their Coulomb repulsion. The resulting Fermi gas, characterized by reduced Coulomb interactions, is modeled as a non-interacting system. The correlation energy is then determined as the difference between the ground-state energies of the original and transformed Hamiltonians, with the former calculated via perturbation theory. The study evaluates the method's performance across various electron densities, comparing its results against standard perturbation theory and other established computational approaches.

This study introduces a method for generating realistic, physically constrained synthetic seismic data by integrating site uncertainty with optimal transport. The primary aim is to enhance the fidelity of machine learning models trained on synthetic data for tasks such as seismic inversion and source localization. The approach begins by creating a synthetic subsurface model and assigning each grid cell a specific site response spectrum. To introduce variability, the method applies covariance inflation to the site response spectra, where the degree of inflation is determined by calculating the optimal transport distance between the spectral density and a predefined target distribution. The resulting synthetic dataset is then used to train a machine learning model for seismic source localization, with performance evaluated against a model trained on ground-truth data. The results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly improves performance, particularly in scenarios involving site response variability.

The rapid expansion of Big Data has created a pressing need for efficient, distributed algorithms to handle large-scale data processing. However, the inherent interconnectedness of Big Data with sensitive information, such as personal details, has intensified the challenge of safeguarding privacy during distributed computations. To address this, we introduce a novel distributed tensor network method that enables decentralized Big Data processing while ensuring data privacy. Our approach employs randomized tensor network decomposition to break down a large tensor into numerous smaller tensors, each containing only a fraction of the original data. Consequently, the resulting computations are performed in a distributed manner, with each local tensor processed independently. To ensure data protection, the randomized decomposition is further fortified by adding random noise to the individual tensors. This technique effectively prevents the reconstruction of the original data from the noisy fragments. Our proposed method is evaluated through extensive experiments on a real-world dataset, demonstrating that it successfully maintains data privacy while achieving efficient distributed computation.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for training robotic policies, yet its practical application remains limited by the "reality gap"—the discrepancy between simulated and real-world environments. This paper introduces SafeAPT, a new framework designed to ensure safe and secure RL training within simulations and facilitate the transfer of policies to real-world scenarios. SafeAPT employs a multi-agent architecture where each agent operates in a distinct simulated environment. By training these agents to maximize the same reward function, the system generates a diverse set of policies. SafeAPT selects the best-performing policy by evaluating it on a real robot, provided the evaluation meets strict safety constraints. This approach allows for the training of policies on real hardware without exposing the physical robot to unsafe behaviors. Furthermore, SafeAPT enforces security by restricting the simulation-to-real deployment to policies that have been trained across varied simulated environments. We validate the framework using a simulated-to-real task involving a mobile robot navigating a maze.

We examine how these features vary across different environments, including intracluster and intragroup gases, as well as in intergalactic and intergalactic medium regions. Additionally, we explore the relationship between these physical properties and the underlying mechanisms driving jet formation and dissipation. This paper introduces a novel, data-driven approach to identifying significant predictors in nonlinear time series regression models, which are prevalent in fields like economics, finance, and engineering. The method employs a new time-inconsistent sieve model, which offers greater flexibility than traditional time-stationary sieves, and utilizes an adaptive inference sieve estimator to pinpoint key variables. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of this estimator, along with its associated stepwise selection and wild bootstrap procedures, under standard regularity conditions. The proposed framework is validated through simulations and applied to real-world datasets, including a time-inconsistent GARCH model for analyzing financial volatility and a nonlinear time-invariant autoregressive model for forecasting US unemployment rates.

Offensive language detection (OvD) is a critical challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with numerous studies focusing on identifying and mitigating such content. While recent advancements have introduced various neural architectures, the impact of specific model choices on performance remains unclear. This paper presents a comparative analysis of different neural frameworks for OvD, utilizing both pre-trained and task-specific models. We evaluate architectures including Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and Transformer variants. Our findings indicate that Transformers equipped with pre-trained language models significantly outperform other neural approaches. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even simple, non-pretrained CNNs can achieve competitive results.

Functional connectivity (FC) is a critical concept in neuroscience, describing the statistical interdependence between distinct brain regions. Although FC has been extensively studied, its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This research introduces a deep learning framework designed to uncover the hidden patterns within FC. The proposed methodology employs a deep learning model to extract latent features from FC matrices, subsequently utilizing clustering techniques to group these latent features. This allows for the identification of distinct clustering patterns in FC, which are then correlated with specific cognitive tasks. The results demonstrate that the discovered latent features effectively capture the essential characteristics of FC, and the resulting clustering patterns align with the underlying cognitive processes.

This study investigates the convergence properties of Nesterov's accelerated method (the "boosted method") applied to smooth, strongly convex, and nonconvex functions within the framework of dissipative theory. The method's dissipativity is analyzed across three distinct metrics: the Euclidean space, the Loewner metric, and the Bregman distance. The authors demonstrate that the sequence of iterates generated by the method is Fejer-monotonic with respect to the set of minimizers, a property that guarantees the convergence of iterates. Additionally, the study establishes that the method achieves an optimal $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ rate of convergence for the objective function values.

This study introduces a new approach for boundary treatment within space-time discontinuous Galerkin methods applied to hyperbolic systems featuring source terms. These methods are known for their high-order accuracy in both space and time, yet they struggle with boundary treatments due to the implicit-explicit nature of the Runge-Kutta scheme used. To address this, the paper proposes a novel technique that bypasses the need to resolve the time-dependent non-linear equations at boundaries. Instead, it utilizes the solution from the preceding time step to determine the boundary values for the current step. Additionally, the authors demonstrate that this boundary treatment does not compromise the method's overall convergence order.

We introduce a new 3D photonic crystal back reflector designed to enhance light absorption in thin and ultra-thin silicon films. This structure, fabricated using a self-assembly technique, consists of a silicon dioxide layer featuring a hexagonal arrangement of air holes. The device is optimized to capture and trap light across the entire solar spectrum. Our analysis demonstrates that the 3D back reflector boosts absorption in the 300–1000 nm silicon layer by 100% and 1000–2000 nm by 100% respectively, compared to a flat silicon layer of the same thickness. The proposed structure is compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing processes and holds significant promise for next-generation photovoltaic technologies.

The paper introduces the credal valuation network (CVN), a probabilistic graphical model designed to facilitate robust multi-agent reasoning under uncertainty. By utilizing valuation algebra, the CVN offers a general framework for expressing uncertainty through set-valued measures, which can be interpreted as credal sets, p-boxes, or Dempster-Shafer belief functions. This work examines the CVN's capacity to represent and conduct inference across various uncertainty scenarios, including those involving ambiguous and incomplete information.

Top-K recommendation has become a standard approach for addressing the challenges of cold-start and data sparsity in recommender systems. However, most existing methods rely on a hard-margin strategy that treats all negative samples as equally detrimental, thereby neglecting their varying degrees of negativity. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel adaptive margin technique that dynamically adjusts penalties based on the specific characteristics of negative samples. Additionally, we propose a probabilistic metric training framework designed to enhance the discriminative power of user and item embeddings. This framework employs a dual-loss strategy combining a margin-based loss to enforce adaptive separation and a probabilistic loss to constrain metric properties. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

The concept of non-Markovianity in quantum channels is examined, with particular attention to channels that are not unitary. We demonstrate that a non-unitary channel exhibits inherent non-Markovianity, meaning it cannot be modeled as a memoryless process. This non-Markovianity is "eternal," persisting regardless of the initial system state or the specific quantum metric used to measure it. This finding is significant because it highlights the crucial role of non-Markovian effects in the modeling of open quantum systems.

This study introduces a framework for effective classification that integrates counterfactual reasoning with active learning. The proposed methodology first identifies counterfactual instances for data points situated near decision boundaries, then employs a weighted voting scheme to assign labels to boundary cases based on these examples. Subsequently, the method is adapted into an active learning context where the voting scheme guides sample selection, prioritizing counterfactual instances deemed most critical for labeling. The approach is evaluated across multiple datasets, demonstrating its efficacy in both the active learning and standard classification settings.

This paper introduces RoSmEEry, a simulation framework designed to evaluate and benchmark semantic mapping algorithms. The system offers a flexible, user-friendly environment for creating diverse scenarios involving various objects and sensor types, enabling the assessment of both individual sensors and their combinations. To facilitate this, we developed a new simulator module that supports advanced features such as LiDAR, RGB-D cameras, and IMUs. Additionally, we created a new semantic mapping module to generate ground truth maps for comparison against the output of evaluated algorithms. We validate RoSmEEry by testing several state-of-the-art semantic mapping techniques and analyzing their performance.

Rikudo, a two-dimensional strategy game developed by the Japanese company DeNA, involves players controlling a single piece on a grid. This game, known as a path-hashing puzzle, requires the player to navigate from a starting point to a target destination without colliding with other pieces. In this study, we demonstrate that determining whether a valid winning path exists for a given piece arrangement is NP-hard.

Optimal Transport (OT) has become a vital instrument in machine learning, enabling the quantification of distributional differences and facilitating the transfer of knowledge across domains. However, OT methods are often hindered by prohibitive computational costs, rendering them impractical for tasks involving massive datasets. This article presents an overview of recent breakthroughs in OT algorithms, highlighting techniques designed to mitigate these computational burdens.

Ramanujan's three modular identities are now recognized as equivalent to the Hecke triangle groups. This paper demonstrates that these identities can be derived by examining the factorization of the generating matrices found within the Hecke groups.

We present new redshift and velocity dispersion measurements for the lensing galaxies in eight quasar systems, utilizing high-resolution spectra from the Keck Observatory. These findings are compared against previously published data from the TDCOSMO project to evaluate the accuracy of the earlier measurements. Our results indicate that the redshifts derived from the new spectra are consistently more accurate than those from the prior observations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the updated velocity dispersion measurements are superior to the older ones, which were hindered by low signal-to-noise ratios. These new data points are essential for calculating the Hubble constant ($H_0$) and refining the lensing mass models. We anticipate that forthcoming observations from the TDCOSMO initiative will yield even more precise velocity dispersion measurements for the lensing galaxies.

The paper presents a novel approach to address nonlinear $q$-fractional differential equations defined on time scales by utilizing the $q$-Hadamard fractional derivative. The study highlights that the $q$-Hadamard derivative is a specific instance of the generalized forward difference operator on time scales, which allows for the derivation of general solutions to $q$-fractional differential and $q$-fractional integral equations when the right-hand side is a continuous function.

The phonon Hall effect (PHE) in crystalline materials lacking inversion symmetry is primarily governed by the interplay of the magnetic field and the material's skew scattering. While the bulk carrier Hall effect is well-understood, the PHE remains elusive. This study demonstrates that the PHE in bulk crystals is characterized by the bulk Chern number, a topological invariant derived from the phonon Berry curvature within the Brillouin zone. This number encapsulates the combined influence of the magnetic field and the crystal structure on the effect. Furthermore, the theory is validated through first-principles calculations on a two-dimensional MoS₂ monolayer, which confirms the topological nature of the PHE.

Nod-and-shuffle (N&S) spectrometers are highly effective for capturing spectra across a wide field of view, as they utilize a single detector to record data from the entire field of view. This capability is achieved by spatially encoding the sky onto a 2D detector, where the third dimension represents spectral information. In this study, we introduce a novel spectral imaging technique that merges N&S with shifted excitation Raman difference spectroscopy (SERDS). SERDS functions by acquiring two spectra from the same target using slightly detuned laser wavelengths; Raman peaks remain stationary while the laser lines shift. This approach effectively eliminates background fluorescence and reduces the influence of Fabry-Perot artifacts. By integrating these methods, we developed a 3D data cube where one axis corresponds to the sky, the second to the spectrum, and the third to the laser frequency shift. This configuration enables the simultaneous elimination of background noise and artifacts while maintaining the high efficiency of the N&S system. We validated this method using laboratory tests on a laboratory lamp and a laboratory lamp.
